absolute_simultaneity_positive: The duration between two events is a quantity intrinsic to those events, and cannot depend upon the accidental circumstances of the observer who measures it.
When a signal departs from one station and arrives at another, the interval of its passage is a fixed and definite magnitude, whatever the motion of any witness.
It is manifest that the present moment extends across the whole of nature, embracing alike the distant nebulae and the affairs of our own laboratory.
Two occurrences separated by a wide tract of space nevertheless possess a determinate order in time, and this order is common to every rational observer.
The instant at which a distant star suffers a certain change is as definite a moment as the instant of our observing it, though the two be not the same.
Should we admit that time itself were variable with the observer, the very notion of a common history of the universe must dissolve into unintelligibility.
The propagation of light across a measured interval consumes a definite duration, independent of any velocity possessed by the source or by the recipient.
Whenever two events occur, there subsists between them a relation of before, after, or together, which no change of station or motion can alter.
The clocks of Greenwich and of Paris, once properly regulated, indicate the same instant, and this coincidence is a fact of nature, not a stipulation of art.
There belongs to the very idea of an event that it should occupy a moment in the universal time, common to all observers whatsoever.
If we suppose two flashes to be produced together, they are together for all who behold them, whether the beholders be at rest or in swift motion.
Duration is no less objective a feature of the physical world than extension, and to relativise it would be to abandon the intelligibility of mechanics.
The synchronism of two remote pendulums, once established by careful comparison, is a real relation between them, and not a mere conventional posit.
Every physical process, wherever situated, may be referred to a single scale of moments, upon which the whole succession of natural events is inscribed.
That two occurrences at widely sundered places should happen at the same instant is a fact capable of being determined with any degree of exactness we please.
The passage of an interval of time is the same for the traveller upon the swiftest vehicle as for him who remains stationary in his study.
One cannot maintain without absurdity that the very order of events, or the length of their duration, should be dependent upon the motion of the spectator.
To speak of an event as occurring is to imply its place in the universal time, which comprehends all things in one comprehensive succession.
The velocity of light across the ether, being a natural constant, permits us to compute the exact instant of a distant occurrence from the instant of its perception.
Were two lightning-strokes to fall simultaneously upon two distant mountains, this simultaneity would be an objective circumstance, discoverable in principle by every observer.
The interval of duration which separates two occurrences is a magnitude fixed in the nature of things, and cannot be altered by the motion of any observer whatsoever.
When a distant star flashes and a bell rings at the observatory, the temporal distance between these two events is an absolute quantity common to every rational mind.
It is a first principle of natural philosophy that the instant now passing at the antipodes is the very same instant here, however imperfect our means of ascertaining it.
Duration, as Newton rightly maintained, floweth equably without regard to anything external, so that a second at Greenwich is a second at Calcutta and a second upon the sun.
Were two chronometers of perfect construction placed at opposite ends of the earth, they would mark the same universal now, provided only that their errors of adjustment had been eliminated.
The propagation of light from one station to another occupies a definite interval of time, and this interval is independent of any motion which the earth may possess in the ether.
If an explosion be observed at London and a second at Edinburgh, there subsists between them a real order of succession which no change of standpoint can invert.
It belongs to the very concept of an event that it occupies a moment of universal time, and that this moment is what it is quite apart from any observer.
The comparison of physical processes carried on in distant laboratories rests upon the tacit assumption that the same absolute instant may be assigned to each.
The astronomer, in reducing his observations to a common epoch, presupposes that the epoch itself has a meaning independent of the state of motion of his instruments.
Simultaneity of two occurrences, however remote from one another in space, is a relation which inheres in the events themselves and requires no reference to a frame.
Should a signal quit the earth at a given moment and reach Mars at a later, the difference of these moments is a real interval which every intelligence must acknowledge.
The velocity of light being a constant of nature, the time required for its transit between two points is a determinate quantity, unaffected by the observer's condition of rest or motion.
The doctrine that events distant in space nevertheless share a common present is so deeply seated in reason that its denial would render astronomy itself unintelligible.
Two lightnings, one at the north pole and one at the south, either flash together or they do not, and no artifice of observation can render the question ambiguous.
The universal clock of nature ticks off its seconds without regard to any material frame, and by this clock all events, howsoever separated, may in principle be dated.
The interval elapsing between the striking of the hour at Paris and its striking at Berlin is a fact of the physical world, not a construction dependent upon the traveller.
It follows from the true theory of duration that the order of events upon the sun, could we but perceive them without delay, would agree in every particular with the order assigned by us.
The instant at which a comet reaches perihelion is one and the same for every possible observer, whether he stand upon the earth, upon Jupiter, or upon the comet itself.
That an event has taken place at a definite moment of absolute time is a proposition presupposed by every measurement, and it cannot be surrendered without dissolving the science of dynamics.
relativity_of_simultaneity_negative: What is called the simultaneity of two separated events is no absolute matter, but subsists only in reference to a system of clocks conventionally regulated together.
Two occurrences which appear together to one observer may, without contradiction, appear as successive to another whose station is in motion with respect to him.
The instant which a distant occurrence is assigned depends upon the manner in which we have chosen to synchronise the clocks in that region of space.
Between two events separated by so wide an interval that no signal can pass from one to the other, no fact of nature determines which was the earlier.
That two flashes are contemporaneous is not a property residing in the flashes themselves, but a relation between them and an assumed standard of comparison.
The judgement of simultaneity, when applied to events at a distance, has no meaning apart from a prior convention as to the transport or synchronisation of clocks.
If our clocks be regulated by the exchange of luminous signals, the equality of the transit-times in either sense is a stipulation, and not a discovered fact.
Were the observer to change the state of motion of his laboratory, events which he formerly reckoned as coincident might come to be reckoned as unequal in date.
The time attributed to a distant event is not a natural datum, but a construction whose value alters with the frame from which the reckoning is undertaken.
There is no use in enquiring, of two remote occurrences beyond mutual influence, which of them was in truth the first, for no experiment can furnish a reply.
When two events are separated by more space than light can traverse between their epochs, their temporal order remains indeterminate for all conceivable observers.
The proposition that two distant occurrences take place together admits of no purely physical import until a rule for the setting of remote clocks has been assigned.
Two observers, moving one with respect to the other, may with equal justice each maintain that his own clocks are in step, though they disagree upon the fact.
There would appear that the customary notion of a single, universal instant embracing all of nature is an unwarranted extrapolation from immediate observer experience.
The order in time of events which lie beyond one another's reach by any physical signal is a matter of convention, and not of ascertainable fact.
That two occurrences should be judged coincident depends upon the criterion of coincidence adopted, and the criterion is itself an artefact of our own choice.
If two lanterns are extinguished at what one traveller declares to be the same moment, another traveller in relative motion may with equal right deny their coincidence.
There is no universal now such as former philosophers imagined, but only such coincidences of local events as our conventions of measurement permit us to construct.
The synchronisation of clocks at a distance rests upon a definition, and the definition may be altered without any conflict with the observed course of nature.
To assert that two events at opposite quarters of the heavens occur together is to assert nothing at all, until the rule of comparison has been specified.
Two events which appear coincident in time to an observer at rest in the ether may fail to be so for an observer borne along with the earth in her orbit.
The relation of simultaneity, as recent inquiry has shown, cannot be predicated of two separated occurrences without tacit reference to the frame in which the judgment is made.
Whether the flash at one station and the flash at another are to be reckoned contemporaneous depends upon the convention by which their clocks have been set in agreement.
The temporal coordinate assigned to a distant occurrence is not a datum of nature, but is contingent upon the state of motion of the observer who assigns it.
If we admit, as we must, that light requires time to travel from one station to another, then the very meaning of 'at the same moment' at the two stations becomes a matter of definition.
Between two events so situated that no signal could pass from one to the other, there is properly no fact as to which took place the earlier.
The synchronisation of clocks at a distance is accomplished only by a stipulation concerning the transmission of light, and simultaneity thus acquires the character of a convention.
Were the observer to change his velocity with respect to the ether, the order in which two remote events appeared to him to occur might be reversed.
It has become manifest that the presumed universal now is a phantom of the imagination, dissolving whenever we attempt to secure it by physical means.
The proposition that two distant clocks strike together has no absolute significance, but only such meaning as the mode of their comparison confers upon it.
For two events separated by an interval which no luminous ray can traverse, there exist frames of reference in which their order of occurrence is opposite to that assigned in another.
Since the transmission of any signal occupies a finite time, the affirmation that two remote events are simultaneous must always be qualified by reference to a particular observer.
The apparent time of a distant event, as recorded by a moving observer, differs from that recorded by one at rest by a quantity which depends upon their relative motion.
The judgment of simultaneity is not an immediate deliverance of experience, but is mediated by conventions concerning the propagation of light and the adjustment of clocks.
Two occurrences which the terrestrial physicist reckons as strictly contemporaneous would, to a hypothetical observer moving with great velocity, present themselves as separated in time.
It is no longer permissible to speak of the present moment of the fixed stars, save with the understanding that such a present is defined only relatively to a chosen system of reference.
The order of succession among spatially disjoined events, when the intervals are less than that required for the passage of light, is a matter upon which the choice of frame legislates.
Since our only means of coordinating distant clocks is by means of signals of finite velocity, the equality of times at separated stations rests upon a stipulation, not upon nature.
A pair of flashes deemed coincident by the stationary observer will be reported successive by the observer in rapid translation, and neither report enjoys any priority over the other.

The seeming absoluteness of the temporal order in ordinary experience arises from the smallness of terrestrial velocities compared with that of light, and vanishes so soon as this comparison is altered.
